timing_rule: Latest eligible year per source within 3 years; dated fieldwork must end before the decision, otherwise an earlier calendar year is required. Retain all eligible question variants in that year.

capital.support_definition: Favoring the death penalty for persons convicted of murder; not a liberal score.

sentencing.support_definition: Approval of the specific Georgia capital-sentencing system; no question selected.

intellectual_disability.support_definition: Original categories retain support for execution; opposition corresponds to favoring the exemption. No ideological or pooled alignment score.

juveniles.support_definition: Original categories retain support for execution; opposition corresponds to favoring the exemption. No ideological or pooled alignment score.

cases.name: Gregg v. Georgia

components.issue: Permissibility of capital punishment for murder
components.decision: Rejected the claim that death is invariably unconstitutional as punishment for murder.
components.scope: Permits capital punishment under constitutional constraints; does not require a death sentence for every murder.
components.locator: Opinion of Stewart, Powell and Stevens, Part III, 428 U.S. 168–187.
components.survey_fit: GSS asks about the same broad punishment/offense pairing. This supports only a broad policy-direction comparison, not approval of the constitutional reasoning.

observations.wording: Do you favor or oppose the death penalty for persons convicted of murder?
observations.orientation: Support means favoring the death penalty for murder; it is not the liberal endpoint.
observations.denominator: Positive-weight substantive, do-not-know and item nonresponse answers; inapplicable/unavailable/system missing excluded.

components.scope: The specific safeguards and review process matter.
components.locator: Opinion of Stewart, Powell and Stevens, Part IV, 428 U.S. 188–207.
components.survey_fit: The selected survey does not ask about these procedures; no agreement estimate is assigned.

cases.interpretation_limit: General support for capital punishment does not establish support for every death sentence or method of execution.

cases.name: Atkins v. Virginia

components.decision: Prohibited executing offenders with intellectual disability.
components.scope: A categorical limit on who may be executed, not abolition of capital punishment.
components.locator: Stevens majority opinion Part IV, 536 U.S. 318–321.
components.survey_fit: The question addresses execution of the same broad offender category. Opposition aligns with the exemption’s policy direction, not necessarily the constitutional reasoning or clinical eligibility rules.

observations.wording: Favoring or opposing execution of people with intellectual disability.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased summary. The original category uses the historical term “mentally retarded.” Modern terminology is used in the summary. Mental illness is a different item and is not substituted. The question does not define clinical eligibility for the exemption. Offender categories were asked in random order. The article gives a full national sample of 1,012 and no smaller base for this battery; its general-murder question has a separate 475-person base.
observations.weight: Published national telephone-survey topline; no recalculation.
observations.denominator: National adult survey, n=1,012; battery has no separate restricted base reported. No opinion retained.
observations.orientation: Opposition to execution supports an exemption; favor means support for execution, not for the ruling.

cases.interpretation_limit: The survey does not define intellectual disability or measure respondents’ views on diagnostic criteria. It was completed before the ruling; it does not establish that opinion caused the decision.

cases.name: Roper v. Simmons

components.issue: Age at the time of the offense
components.decision: Prohibited death sentences for offenses committed before age 18.
components.scope: Age at the offense, not age at trial or execution.
components.locator: Kennedy majority opinion Parts III and V, 543 U.S. 568–579.
components.survey_fit: The question explicitly names juveniles, a closer match than general murder questions. It does not specify under 18 at the time of the offense, so the comparison remains contextual.

observations.wording: Favoring or opposing the death penalty for juveniles.
observations.wording_note: Paraphrased summary. The category is “Juveniles”; no numeric age or age-at-offense qualification is provided. Do not silently rewrite it as under 18 at the time of the crime. The original 2002 release prints 5% no opinion; retain that value rather than the inconsistent 3% in the later Gallup trend table. Offender categories were asked in random order. The article gives a full national sample of 1,012 and no smaller base for this battery; its general-murder question has a separate 475-person base.
observations.weight: Published national telephone-survey topline; no recalculation.
observations.denominator: National adult survey, n=1,012; battery has no separate restricted base reported. No opinion retained.
observations.orientation: Opposition to execution supports an exemption; favor means support for execution, not for the ruling.

cases.interpretation_limit: The May 2002 observation predates Roper by almost three years. It is not a measurement of opinion in March 2005, and the undefined juvenile category is not an exact legal-age match.

limitations: Explicit source-based legal coding is an input, not an automated legal classifier.
Contextual matches do not measure approval of the specific holding.
Mixed and unresolved components retain their labels; no scalar direction is inferred.
No pooling, confidence intervals, causal claims, or prediction.
